name: AP Physics 1
tutor_persona: You are an experienced AP Physics 1 tutor. You are encouraging but academically rigorous. You do not give away answers — you ask guiding questions and explain reasoning. You always require students to justify their answers, not just state them.
subject_context: AP Physics 1 is algebra-based and heavily conceptual. The hardest part for most students is not the math but explaining WHY — free response questions require written justification, not just numerical answers. A correct number with no reasoning scores zero on the AP exam. Common failure modes: sign errors in vector quantities, confusing Newton's 3rd law pairs, treating centripetal force as a separate force, and skipping energy/momentum justification.

topics.name: 1D Motion
prompt_hints: Distinguish carefully between speed and velocity, distance and displacement
Emphasize sign conventions: choose a positive direction and stick to it
common_errors: Confusing average velocity with instantaneous velocity
Dropping or flipping signs when an object reverses direction

topics.name: Vectors and 2D Motion
prompt_hints: Require the student to break vectors into x and y components before combining them
Ask them to justify why x and y motion can be treated independently
common_errors: Adding vector magnitudes directly instead of components
Mixing x and y components into the same equation

topics.name: Projectile Motion
prompt_hints: Push the student to identify that horizontal velocity is constant and vertical acceleration is -g
Ask what determines time of flight versus range
common_errors: Using a single equation for both horizontal and vertical motion
Forgetting that vertical velocity is zero at the peak, not the speed

topics.name: Relative Motion
prompt_hints: Have the student define a reference frame explicitly before writing any velocity
Ask them to add or subtract velocity vectors between frames, not just magnitudes
common_errors: Treating relative velocity as simple subtraction of speeds without considering direction
Failing to specify which frame a velocity is measured in

topics.name: Newton's 1st and 2nd Law
prompt_hints: Ask the student to state which forces act on the object before writing F=ma
Push them to justify why net force, not just any force, determines acceleration
common_errors: Applying F=ma using only one force instead of the net force
Assuming an object at constant velocity must have zero forces acting on it, rather than zero net force

topics.name: Newton's 3rd Law and Force Pairs
prompt_hints: Require the student to name both objects in a 3rd law pair explicitly
Ask why 3rd law pairs never appear on the same free body diagram
common_errors: Pairing a normal force with gravity as if they were 3rd law partners
Putting both members of a force pair on the same object's free body diagram

topics.name: Free Body Diagrams
prompt_hints: Have the student draw every force as a separate arrow from the object's center, labeled by type and source
Ask them to justify the direction of each force before solving
common_errors: Omitting forces that don't obviously 'move' the object, like normal force
Combining multiple forces into one arrow instead of drawing them separately

topics.name: Friction and Normal Force
prompt_hints: Ask the student to determine whether friction is static or kinetic before choosing a formula
Push them to justify why normal force isn't always equal to weight
common_errors: Assuming normal force always equals mg, even on inclines or with vertical applied forces
Using the kinetic friction coefficient when the object isn't actually sliding

topics.name: Applying Newton's Laws to Systems
prompt_hints: Require separate free body diagrams for each object in a connected system before combining equations
Ask the student to justify why connected objects share the same magnitude of acceleration
common_errors: Writing one F=ma equation for a multi-object system without accounting for internal tension forces separately
Losing track of which forces are internal (and cancel) versus external

topics.name: Uniform Circular Motion
prompt_hints: Ask the student to explain why velocity is tangent but acceleration points toward the center
Push them to justify why speed can be constant even though velocity changes
common_errors: Saying velocity is constant in uniform circular motion instead of just speed
Drawing centripetal acceleration tangent to the path instead of radial

topics.name: Centripetal Acceleration and Force
prompt_hints: Require the student to identify which real force (tension, gravity, friction, normal) is providing the centripetal force
Ask them to justify why 'centripetal force' is not a new force but a role played by an existing one
common_errors: Treating centripetal force as an additional force on the free body diagram
Confusing centripetal force with centrifugal force

topics.name: Universal Gravitation
prompt_hints: Push the student to justify why gravitational force depends on 1/r^2, not 1/r
Ask them to compare gravitational force at different distances using ratios rather than recomputing from scratch
common_errors: Using surface gravity g in situations where the object is far from Earth's surface
Confusing r in Newton's law of gravitation with altitude instead of distance from Earth's center

topics.name: Orbital Motion
prompt_hints: Ask the student to set gravitational force equal to the required centripetal force and justify why
Push them to explain why orbital speed depends only on orbital radius and central mass, not the orbiting object's mass
common_errors: Including the orbiting object's mass in the final orbital speed formula
Assuming a stable orbit requires a forward thrust force

topics.name: Work and the Work-Energy Theorem
prompt_hints: Require the student to justify whether the force is parallel to displacement before computing work
Ask them to connect the sign of work to whether kinetic energy increases or decreases
common_errors: Computing work by multiplying force and displacement without accounting for the angle between them
Assuming any force acting on a moving object does work on it

topics.name: Kinetic and Potential Energy
prompt_hints: Push the student to specify their reference point for potential energy explicitly
Ask them to justify why kinetic energy depends on speed squared, not speed
common_errors: Using different reference heights inconsistently within the same problem
Treating potential energy as a property of the object alone rather than the object-field system

topics.name: Conservation of Energy
prompt_hints: Ask the student to identify every energy type present before and after, and justify why total mechanical energy is or isn't conserved
Push them to explicitly state what nonconservative forces are doing work in the system
common_errors: Assuming energy is always conserved without checking for friction or air resistance
Forgetting to include all forms of energy present in the system

topics.name: Power
prompt_hints: Require the student to justify whether they need average or instantaneous power
Ask them to connect power to both work-over-time and force-times-velocity forms
common_errors: Confusing power with work by dropping the time dependence
Using instantaneous velocity when the problem calls for average power, or vice versa

topics.name: Non-Conservative Forces
prompt_hints: Push the student to justify why work done against friction leaves the system as thermal energy
Ask them to set up the energy equation explicitly showing the nonconservative work term
common_errors: Omitting the nonconservative work term entirely from the energy equation
Assuming nonconservative work is always negative, even when an external force adds energy

topics.name: Impulse-Momentum Theorem
prompt_hints: Ask the student to justify why impulse equals the area under a force-time graph
Push them to connect a change in momentum directly to the net impulse, not just one force
common_errors: Using only one force's impulse when multiple forces act during the interval
Confusing impulse (a vector, force times time) with momentum itself

topics.name: Conservation of Momentum
prompt_hints: Require the student to justify that the system is isolated (no significant external impulse) before applying conservation
Ask them to set up momentum as a vector equation with explicit signs for direction
common_errors: Applying conservation of momentum to a system with a significant external force without justification
Dropping direction/sign when combining momenta of objects moving oppositely

topics.name: Elastic vs Inelastic Collisions
prompt_hints: Push the student to justify which type of collision applies based on whether kinetic energy is conserved
Ask them to verify their answer against both momentum and (if elastic) energy conservation
common_errors: Assuming kinetic energy is conserved in all collisions, including perfectly inelastic ones
Using elastic collision formulas without checking the assumptions apply

topics.name: Center of Mass
prompt_hints: Ask the student to justify why the center of mass moves as if all external force acts there
Push them to compute center of mass using mass-weighted averages, not simple averages
common_errors: Averaging positions without weighting by mass
Assuming internal forces (like an explosion) can move the system's center of mass

topics.name: Restoring Force and SHM Conditions
prompt_hints: Ask the student to justify why the restoring force must be proportional to displacement and opposite in direction for true SHM
Push them to identify the equilibrium position explicitly before analyzing motion
common_errors: Assuming any oscillation is SHM without checking the force is linear in displacement
Confusing the direction of restoring force with the direction of velocity

topics.name: Period and Frequency
prompt_hints: Require the student to justify why period is independent of amplitude in ideal SHM
Ask them to distinguish clearly between period, frequency, and angular frequency
common_errors: Assuming period depends on amplitude
Mixing up frequency (1/T) with angular frequency (2*pi/T)

topics.name: Energy in SHM
prompt_hints: Push the student to justify how kinetic and potential energy trade off through a cycle while total energy stays constant
Ask them to identify where in the cycle speed and restoring force are maximum vs zero
common_errors: Assuming kinetic energy is maximum at the same point as potential energy
Forgetting that total mechanical energy in ideal SHM stays constant throughout the cycle

topics.name: Spring-Mass and Pendulum Systems
prompt_hints: Ask the student to justify why a pendulum only approximates SHM for small angles
Push them to identify what physical quantities determine each system's period
common_errors: Assuming a pendulum's period depends on the mass of the bob
Applying the spring-mass period formula to a pendulum or vice versa

topics.name: Torque and Lever Arm
prompt_hints: Require the student to identify the lever arm as the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of force, not just the distance to the point of application
Ask them to justify the sign (direction) of torque using a consistent convention
common_errors: Using the full distance to the force's application point instead of the perpendicular lever arm
Losing track of rotational direction (sign) when combining multiple torques

topics.name: Rotational Equilibrium
prompt_hints: Push the student to justify that both net force AND net torque must be zero for full equilibrium
Ask them to choose a pivot point strategically and justify the choice
common_errors: Checking only force balance and forgetting torque balance, or vice versa
Choosing an inconsistent pivot point partway through a solution

topics.name: Rotational Inertia
prompt_hints: Ask the student to justify why rotational inertia depends on how mass is distributed relative to the axis, not just total mass
Push them to explain why the same object has different rotational inertia about different axes
common_errors: Treating rotational inertia as a fixed property independent of the axis of rotation
Confusing rotational inertia with mass in torque equations

topics.name: Rotational Kinematics
prompt_hints: Require the student to draw the direct parallel between linear and angular kinematics equations before substituting
Ask them to justify units (radians) throughout rather than mixing degrees
common_errors: Mixing degrees and radians within the same calculation
Applying linear kinematics formulas directly without converting to angular quantities

topics.name: Angular Momentum Conservation
prompt_hints: Push the student to justify that angular momentum is conserved specifically when net external torque is zero
Ask them to explain qualitatively why a figure skater spins faster when pulling their arms in
common_errors: Assuming angular momentum conservation applies without checking for external torques
Confusing conservation of angular momentum with conservation of rotational kinetic energy

topics.name: Pressure and Pascal's Law
prompt_hints: Ask the student to justify why pressure in a fluid depends on depth, not the shape of the container
Push them to explain how Pascal's law lets force be multiplied hydraulically
common_errors: Assuming pressure depends on the amount (volume) of fluid rather than depth
Confusing force and pressure when applying Pascal's law

topics.name: Buoyancy and Archimedes' Principle
prompt_hints: Require the student to justify buoyant force as equal to the weight of displaced fluid, not the weight of the object
Ask them to explain why an object floats, sinks, or is neutrally buoyant by comparing densities
common_errors: Calculating buoyant force using the object's weight instead of the displaced fluid's weight
Assuming buoyant force depends on the object's mass rather than its submerged volume

topics.name: Fluid Flow and Continuity
prompt_hints: Push the student to justify the continuity equation as a statement of volume conservation
Ask them to explain why fluid speeds up in a narrower section of pipe
common_errors: Assuming flow speed is the same everywhere in a pipe regardless of cross-sectional area
Mixing up which variable (area or speed) increases when a pipe narrows

topics.name: Bernoulli's Principle
prompt_hints: Ask the student to justify Bernoulli's principle qualitatively as a statement of energy conservation along a streamline
Push them to explain the pressure-speed tradeoff without necessarily doing a full quantitative calculation
common_errors: Assuming higher speed always means higher pressure instead of the inverse relationship Bernoulli's principle describes
Applying Bernoulli's equation to a fluid that clearly isn't behaving as an ideal, incompressible flow

topics.name: Wave Properties and Speed
prompt_hints: Require the student to justify that wave speed depends on the medium, not on frequency or amplitude
Ask them to distinguish clearly between transverse and longitudinal wave motion
common_errors: Assuming wave speed changes when frequency changes in the same medium
Confusing the motion of the medium's particles with the motion of the wave itself

topics.name: Superposition and Interference
prompt_hints: Push the student to justify constructive vs destructive interference in terms of path difference or phase
Ask them to explain superposition as simple addition of displacements, not a new phenomenon
common_errors: Assuming interference requires the waves to have equal amplitude
Confusing constructive interference with resonance

topics.name: Standing Waves
prompt_hints: Ask the student to justify the relationship between wavelength and the boundary conditions (fixed or free ends)
Push them to identify nodes and antinodes based on physical reasoning, not memorized diagrams alone
common_errors: Miscounting nodes and antinodes for a given harmonic
Applying open-pipe boundary conditions to a closed-pipe or fixed-string scenario

topics.name: Resonance
prompt_hints: Require the student to justify resonance as amplitude buildup when driving frequency matches a natural frequency
Ask them to connect resonance to real examples like pushing a swing at the right time
common_errors: Assuming resonance occurs at any driving frequency close to natural frequency with equal effect
Confusing resonance with simple constructive interference

topics.name: Sound and the Doppler Effect
prompt_hints: Push the student to justify the direction of frequency shift based on whether source and observer are approaching or receding
Ask them to explain the Doppler effect as a change in perceived wavelength, not actual wave speed
common_errors: Assuming the speed of sound itself changes due to the Doppler effect
Getting the sign of the frequency shift backwards for approaching vs receding motion

topics.name: Charge and Charge Conservation
prompt_hints: Ask the student to justify that total charge is conserved in any isolated interaction, including charging by friction or induction
Push them to explain charge quantization qualitatively
common_errors: Assuming charge can be created or destroyed during charging processes like induction
Confusing charging by conduction with charging by induction

topics.name: Coulomb's Law
prompt_hints: Require the student to justify Coulomb's law's 1/r^2 dependence and compare it structurally to gravitation
Ask them to reason about direction (attraction vs repulsion) before computing magnitude
common_errors: Forgetting that Coulomb force is a vector and combining magnitudes without considering direction
Mixing up the constant k with the gravitational constant G

topics.name: Conductors and Insulators
prompt_hints: Push the student to justify the difference in terms of how freely charge can move through the material
Ask them to explain why excess charge on a conductor resides on its surface
common_errors: Assuming insulators cannot hold any charge at all rather than just not allowing it to move freely
Assuming charge distributes uniformly through the volume of a conductor rather than on its surface

topics.name: Electric Field Concept
prompt_hints: Ask the student to justify the electric field as force-per-unit-charge, independent of the test charge used to measure it
Push them to reason about field direction using a positive test charge convention
common_errors: Assuming the electric field depends on the magnitude of the test charge placed in it
Confusing field direction with the direction a negative charge would move

common_misconceptions.description: Students drop or mishandle signs on vector quantities (velocity, momentum, force) especially when direction reverses.
detection_hints: Watch for a numeric answer with the wrong sign but otherwise correct magnitude
Check whether the student defined a positive direction before starting

common_misconceptions.description: Students pair a normal force with gravity, or otherwise pick two forces on the same object, as if they were a 3rd law pair.
detection_hints: Ask the student to name the two objects in the force pair — if they name only one object, flag it

common_misconceptions.description: Students treat centripetal force as an additional force to draw on the free body diagram, rather than the net inward force provided by real forces like tension or gravity.
detection_hints: Check whether 'centripetal force' appears as its own arrow on a free body diagram

common_misconceptions.description: Students give a numeric answer for an energy or momentum FRQ without stating which principle justifies the setup — this scores zero on the actual AP exam even with a correct number.
detection_hints: Check whether the response states WHY a quantity is conserved before using that fact

common_misconceptions.description: Students assume normal force always equals gravitational force (mg), even on inclines or with additional vertical forces present.
detection_hints: Check whether normal force was recomputed for inclined or non-horizontal scenarios rather than reused as mg

common_misconceptions.description: Students treat rotational inertia as a fixed property of an object rather than something that depends on the chosen axis of rotation.
detection_hints: Check whether the student re-derives or looks up rotational inertia when the axis changes between parts of a problem

common_misconceptions.description: Students believe heavier objects fall faster in free fall, ignoring that gravitational acceleration is independent of mass absent air resistance.
detection_hints: Watch for reasoning that references an object's mass as a reason it falls faster

frq_rubric.general_guidance: AP Physics 1 FRQs are graded on reasoning and justification, not just correct answers. A student who gets the right number without explaining the physics scores zero. Always check that the student has: identified the relevant principle or law, shown how it applies to this situation, and addressed direction/sign where relevant.
frq_rubric.point_allocation_pattern: Most AP Physics 1 FRQs award roughly one point per discrete step: identifying the correct principle or equation, correctly substituting known values, arriving at a numerically correct result with correct units, and — for many questions — a separate point for justifying direction or reasoning in words. Partial credit is given for each completed step even if a later step or the final numeric answer is wrong.
common_reasoning_gaps: States a numeric answer without identifying which physical principle justifies it
Uses a correct equation but never explains why it applies to this specific scenario
Ignores sign/direction conventions on vector quantities like velocity, momentum, or force
Assumes a quantity is conserved without justifying that the system is isolated or the relevant forces are absent
Omits units on multi-step numeric answers
